title: Feeling the inside
hookLine: interoception, sensing the inner body, is linked to recognizing emotions

lines: A KNOCK, A FLUTTER, OR NOTHING.
cards: A quick test, no equipment needed. Without touching your wrist or your neck, without a hand on your chest, can you find your heartbeat right now, just from the inside? Some people find it at once, a steady knock.

Some find a faint flutter. Some find nothing at all, and that happens too. Researchers use a version of this test in the lab, to study a sense that rarely gets a name, one that points inward instead of out.
A new week on attention starts by turning it around.

teach.b: The name is interoception: sensing the inner state of the body. A heartbeat, a breath, hunger, a full bladder, a knot in the stomach, warmth in the face.
Sight and hearing tell you about the world; interoception tells you about the weather inside.
In one common lab method, people silently count their heartbeats for a short stretch without feeling for a pulse, and their count is compared with the real one. People differ quite a bit.
Some studies have linked better heartbeat sensing with stronger or clearer emotional experience, and with recognizing emotions more easily. The honest limit: the counting test has critics.
Some researchers argue people partly guess from what they know about heart rates rather than truly sensing the beat.

teach.h: A LEAD, NOT A SETTLED FACT.
teach.b: So the link is a lead the science is still following, not a settled fact. Underneath sits an older idea.
The American psychologist William James argued that emotion and the body are bound up far more tightly than people assume.
In his Principles of Psychology he put it in a backwards-sounding way: "we feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble."
Later scientists disputed parts of his theory, but his hunch, that the body is part of how a feeling is known, sits close to what interoception research explores now.
Some contemplative traditions begin in the same place: the breath, the belly, the body, felt from inside.

how: Body scans in mindfulness courses and breath-focused practice in several contemplative traditions train attention on inner sensation; researchers study the same ability with heartbeat-sensing tasks.

sensing the body's inner state, like heartbeat or hunger
a feeling of guilt that settles deep inside

it's the sense of the body's inner state: heartbeat, breath, hunger, tension.

games.q: you're in a lab, asked to count your heartbeats for a short stretch. what are you allowed to do?
o: press two fingers to your wrist.
sit still and sense it from the inside.
watch a heart monitor and copy it.
games.why: no hands: you count from the inside, and your count is compared with the real one. people differ quite a bit.

practice: Without touching anything, see if you can find your heartbeat from the inside, in the chest, the throat, the fingertips, the ears, and if you do, count a few beats and then just listen.
If you can't, that's fine: feel what is there instead, the breath, warmth, pressure, a pulse somewhere unexpected, and place a hand on your chest any time it helps.

wordCard.voice: Feeling the inside. Interoception: the sense of the body's inner state, heartbeat, breath, hunger, tension, which some studies link to recognizing emotions. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the inside. Sight looks out at the world; this quiet sense looks in. Until tomorrow.
